questions.title: How can the Federal Circuit reverse a jury’s infringement verdict under the substantial evidence standard based on self-contradictory expert testimony?
questions.question_body: The panel says it reviews JMOL denials under Fifth Circuit law and looks for substantial evidence supporting the verdict. Yet it reverses because the patentee’s expert gave confusing, self-contradictory testimony about what signals met the claim limitations, citing Johns Hopkins v. Datascope. I thought weighing credibility was for the jury. Under what circumstances can the appellate court deem an expert’s testimony legally insufficient (rather than just confusing) and conclude that no reasonable jury could rely on it?

questions.title: For the ’134 patent, do the ‘interference generating signals’ have to be physically present at the ADC input, or can a downstream modeled PIM signal satisfy limitation 1[a]?
questions.question_body: Claim 1[a] requires over-sampling a passband of received signals that includes both signals of interest and interference generating signals. The patentee’s expert mapped the ‘interference generating signals’ to a modeled PIM path that is created after the RF ADC in an FPGA. The panel held that cannot satisfy limitation 1[a] because you cannot sample a signal that does not yet exist. Could the ‘interference generating signals’ instead be the actual RF interference present at the receiver front-end (even if the model is generated later), and if so, what level of explicit testimony or mapping is required at trial to tie those pre-ADC signals to the claim language?

questions.title: Does ‘three signals S1, S2 and S3’ in the ’775 patent require three unique inputs, and how did the court treat the prosecution amendment from ‘two or three signals’?
questions.question_body: The district court construed ‘three signals’ as ‘separately identifiable’ but not necessarily unique, relying in part on inventor testimony. On appeal, the panel said there was no clear and unambiguous disclaimer even though the patentee amended from ‘two or three signals’ to ‘three signals.’ What is the doctrinal threshold for finding clear and unmistakable prosecution disclaimer in this context, and when can ‘three signals’ be satisfied by two unique sources plus a copy or preprocessed version of one of them?

questions.title: What exactly must be proven to meet the ’775 claim’s requirement of seven third-order multiplications, especially when the accused design uses modulus and conjugate operations?
questions.question_body:
The claim requires generating seven specific third-order products of S1, S2, and S3. The Nokia documentation showed only three distinct products and involved |x| and complex conjugate operations. The panel found no evidence of all seven multiplications or a valid mapping. I’m unsure about: 
- Do the seven listed combinations require seven distinct computed products, or can a single computed product correspond to multiple listed permutations due to commutativity/associativity? 
- Can |x| or x′ be treated as the same ‘signal’ for purposes of S1/S2/S3, or does using modulus/conjugate move the operation outside the scope of ‘digitally multiplying’ the claimed signals? 
- If the accused system computes ten polynomial terms p(n)=a0..a9, what kind of trial proof is needed to identify which seven align with the claim’s seven products?

questions.title: What must be preserved in a Rule 50(a) motion to avoid waiver on appeal for a claim-limitation challenge like ‘three signals,’ and do claim construction or summary judgment arguments count?
questions.question_body:
The district court said defendants waived the argument that S1, S2, S3 must be unique by not raising it in Rule 50(a). The Federal Circuit reversed on a different ground (failure to prove the seven multiplications). For preservation: 
- Is it enough in Rule 50(a) to generally assert ‘no substantial evidence supports element X,’ or must the movant specify the exact construction theory (e.g., ‘unique signals’)? 
- If a party argued a construction at claim construction or summary judgment, does that preserve it for JMOL? 
- How do courts distinguish between waiving a legal construction argument and preserving a factual sufficiency challenge tied to that element?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate (rather than reverse) the damages award after finding no infringement, and what happens to the jury’s validity findings?
questions.question_body: The panel reversed the denial of JMOL of noninfringement on all asserted claims and then vacated the $166M lump-sum damages award. If there is now a judgment of noninfringement on all asserted claims, is there any scenario in which damages could be reinstated on remand? Also, the jury found the claims valid. Do those validity findings remain in the judgment with any preclusive effect, or are they effectively moot because there is no liability?

questions.title: Was it appropriate for the district court to rely on inventor testimony to support a construction that ‘three signals’ need not be unique under Phillips and related precedent?
questions.question_body: The claim says ‘three signals S1, S2 and S3,’ and the district court relied in part on inventor testimony to conclude they are ‘separately identifiable’ but not unique. My understanding is that inventor testimony is extrinsic and generally less reliable than the intrinsic record. Did the Federal Circuit endorse this use of inventor testimony, or simply find it non-dispositive given the intrinsic record? More broadly, when is it proper to lean on inventor testimony to add a qualifier like ‘separately identifiable’ that is not in the claim text?
